Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/3. Mastering Data Consistency Across Microservices.md
- Microservices operate with independent databases, making data consistency challenging. However, ensuring consistency is crucial for reliability, user trust, and preventing financial or operational errors. - Different types of consistency models can be explored while designing the services. - Strong consistency ensures immediate accuracy but impacts performance. - Eventual consistency allows temporary inconsistencies but improves scalability. - Causal consistency maintains event order across services. - Read-your-writes consistency ensures users see their updates immediately. - Multiple strategies can be used to facilitate data consistency across services. - Synchronous communication provides strong consistency but can cause bottlenecks. - Asynchronous messaging improves scalability but requires handling eventual consistency. - Choreography and Orchestration ensure consistency by handling distributed transactions with compensating actions. - An event-driven architecture enables eventual consistency through event sourcing and CQRS. - Change Data Capture (CDC) streams database changes to ensure real-time consistency.

However, due to this separation, a major challenge with microservices is maintaining data consistency. In a monolithic system, all functionalities share a single database, resulting in consistent updates. On the other hand, microservices architecture advocates that each service should manage its database. While this is a good practice, it can lead to some scenarios such as:

In a choreography-based approach, microservices communicate through events without a central controller. Each service listens for specific events and performs its task upon receiving a relevant event. If a service fails, it emits a compensation event to roll back prior changes.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/5. Apache Kafka/Apache Kafka® Tiered Storage in Depth - How Writes and Metadata Flow.md
Aiven, being a managed Kafka provider, built extra tooling around tiered storage in their control plane. Their system reads the metadata topic from all clusters to build a materialized view per service that powers:

- Copy threads (remote.log.manager.copier.thread.pool.size): you could have 10 copy threads configured, meaning at most 10 segments could be uploaded concurrently - Plugin rate limit (upload.rate.limit.bytes.per.second: could be 100 MB/s - Broker rate limit (remote.log.manager.copy.max.bytes.per.second): could be double the plugin rate, so as to limit the amount of files that will make it through to the plugin and compete between each other at the plugin rate limit. The Upload

- It must not be an active segment. (You can’t have producers actively writing to it). - Has all of the required index files created - the time index file, the offset index file, the producer snapshot index, the leader epoch index, and the transaction index. - Has not been uploaded to the external store before (obviously). - The Last Stable Offset (LSO) must have advanced beyond this file’s largest offset. - Reminder: the LSO is a composite of the High Watermark and the last (highest) committed offset for transactions - it represents the minimum of both. It basically represents the highest (latest) offset that should be visible to consumers - It’s used to ensure that all in-sync brokers have replicated the data by the time we tier it, as well as ensure that all transactions up to that point have been committed.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/1. A Comprehensive Guide to Database Sharding.md
As data volume increases, you can add more shards to accommodate the growth. But it’s not only about scalability. By distributing the query load across multiple machines, sharding can significantly improve response times and overall system throughput.

2. _Shard-Aware Server. C_lients can contact any node using a load balancer. If the contacted node is responsible for the requested shard, it can handle the request itself. Otherwise, the request will be forwarded to the appropriate shard, and the response will be routed back to the client. This method is relatively simple to implement but can introduce extra network hops if the initial node doesn't own the required data.

To work around that, data needs to be split into pieces called shards, small enough to fit into individual nodes. As an additional benefit, the system's capacity for handling requests also increases since the load of accessing the data is spread over more nodes.

One way of fixing this is to have different read modes. Eventually consistent reads go to a replica, whereas strongly consistent reads will be handled by the primary node. An alternative is to wait until all the replicas have gotten the write before acknowledging it as being completed to the user.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/5. Apache Kafka/Apache Kafka® Tiered Storage in Depth - How Writes and Metadata Flow.md
1. The broker decides it’ll tier a local segment. It creates a unique UUID for the **remote** log segment. It creates a metadata record with a state of COPY_STARTED and produces it durably to the internal Kafka topic. 2. It uploads the data via the plugin. The plugin returns a set of custom metadata specific to the plugin (KIP-917). 3. A new record referring to the same remote segment UUID, this time with an updated COPY_FINISHED state, is persisted in the Kafka topic. It also contains the plugin metadata.

- The unique UUID of the remote segment and the topic-partition it relates to - e.g {topic}-{topic-uuid}-{partition}-{remote-segment-uuid} - The offsets this segment **starts** and **ends** at. - The broker ID which uploaded it. - The state of the segment - which can either be COPY_STARTED, COPY_FINISHED or DELETE_STARTED, DELETE_FINISHED. There’s a simple state machine for this. - An index mapping of offsets to leader epochs in this segment. - Some extra stuff I won’t mention.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/3. Mastering Data Consistency Across Microservices.md
- **Increased Latency:** If a service takes longer to respond, the entire request chain is delayed. - **Reduced Availability:** If one service is down, dependent services cannot proceed. This can result in a system-wide failure. - **Tight Coupling:** Services become interdependent, making deployments and changes more complex.

Data consistency in microservices refers to the guarantee that all services in a system see the same data at the same time.

- A user places an order, but the system doesn’t acknowledge the user, causing a duplicate order when the user places the order again. - A user checks their bank balance, and it shows different amounts on the mobile app and the website. - A user books a travel ticket, but due to an inconsistency, two people are assigned the same seat.

- If accuracy is critical, use strong consistency (for example, banking, and inventory management). - If speed and availability matter more than real-time accuracy, use eventual consistency (for example, social media, and analytics dashboards). - If ordering is important, use causal consistency (for example, chat applications). - If users should see their updates immediately, use read-your-writes consistency (for example, shopping carts, and profile settings). questions.question: Compare range-based, hash-based, and directory-based sharding.
questions.core_answer: Range sharding is simple and helps range scans but can hotspot. Hash sharding spreads load better but hurts locality. Directory sharding is most flexible, but it adds a lookup layer and more operational complexity.
questions.deep_dive:
Range-based sharding is simple and efficient for range scans, but it can create hotspots if new or popular data clusters into one range. Hash-based sharding usually spreads keys more evenly, but it makes range queries and some locality-sensitive workloads much harder. Directory-based sharding gives the most flexibility because a lookup service decides where keys live, but that adds another dependency and another hop. The right choice depends on your query pattern more than on elegance.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/1. A Comprehensive Guide to Database Sharding.md
The advantage of range-based sharding is that it is simple. The application can quickly determine which shard to write to or read from based on the value of the sharding key. It also makes range queries efficient. You know exactly which shard to query if you need all users with IDs between 1,500,000 and 1,800,000. To make range scans fast, each shard is generally stored in sorted order on the disk.

There are several ways to map data to shards. We'll explore the four main types: range-based, hash-based, relationship-based, and directory-based sharding.

Range-based sharding splits up the data by sorting the values in one or more columns in lexicographic order and using ranges of such values. For example, you might divide a user database based on user ID ranges or a product database based on price, etc.

Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to deterministically map the shard key to a seemingly random number (a hash value) within a specific range. The hash value determines which shard the data goes to.
notes: Interview framing: Choose based on access pattern, not elegance.
Always justify shard-key choice with real access patterns and cardinality distribution.
Discuss resharding and migration cost before claiming long-term scalability.
Mention hotspot detection and mitigation in both data and traffic paths.

questions.question: What does CAP mean in practical production terms?
questions.core_answer: During a partition you choose whether to reject work to preserve correctness or stay available and accept temporary inconsistency. The right choice depends on whether bad data is worse than an error.
questions.deep_dive:
In practice, CAP is about what failure mode you accept during a network partition. If incorrect data is worse than errors, you bias toward CP and reject or block operations you cannot verify safely. If staying responsive matters more than immediate global correctness, you bias toward AP and accept temporary inconsistency. The practical skill is mapping business requirements to those trade-offs instead of reciting theory. Payments, inventory, and auth usually lean CP; feeds and analytics can often lean AP.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Important Notes.md
**CP or AP?** When a partition happens, you answer one question: Is it worse to show wrong data or no data? - If wrong data is worse = CP (Consistency + Partition tolerance) - If no data is worse = AP (Availability + Partition tolerance) Everything else is implementation.

**The constraint:** You can't have strong consistency, high availability, and partition tolerance at the same time during a network split. You have to choose which pain you'll accept.

**When CP makes sense:** **Money:** balances, wallets, payments You can't double-charge users. Better to fail the transaction. **Inventory:** tickets, limited stock, reservations You can't sell 110 seats on a 100-seat flight. **Security:** permissions, auth tokens, access control An expired token must not work. Ever. **The trade-off:** If the network is broken, some operations fail. But you never silently break correctness.

**Example: Social media app** **Login / password changes = CP** Token revocation must be instant. Better to block than let old tokens work. **Order placement / payments = CP** No double-charges. No overselling. Block if you're not sure. **Like counts / badges → AP** "2 unread" instead of "3 unread" for a few seconds? Fine. **Activity feed → AP** Slightly stale feed is okay if the app stays snappy. **The skill:** Knowing where you can tolerate AP, and where you must enforce CP.

questions.question: How would you explain read-your-writes, causal consistency, and eventual consistency to a product team?
questions.core_answer: Read-your-writes means a user sees their own update immediately. Causal consistency preserves logical ordering between related actions. Eventual consistency means the system converges later, which is fine for some domains but risky for money or inventory.
questions.deep_dive:
Strong consistency means everyone sees the latest committed write immediately, which is useful for money and inventory but more expensive and availability-sensitive. Eventual consistency means replicas or services converge later, which is often acceptable for feeds, notifications, and analytics. Causal consistency preserves logical ordering between related operations, which is important in chat or collaborative systems. Read-your-writes gives a user the guarantee that their own update is visible to them immediately even if the broader system is still converging.

questions.question: Redis high performance?
questions.core_answer: Single-threaded event loop, in-memory, efficient structures, I/O multiplexing, pipelining.
questions.deep_dive:
Redis keeps its working set in memory, which removes disk from the read path for normal operations. It also offers efficient built-in data structures and executes commands atomically in a largely single-threaded command-processing model, which avoids a lot of locking and coordination overhead. For many workloads, the absence of context-switch-heavy concurrency inside the data path is a feature rather than a limitation. The real bottlenecks often shift to network bandwidth, memory pressure, persistence settings, or bad command choices instead of pure CPU.

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis Notes.md
Redis is a memory-based database, and the read and write operations on data are all completed in the memory, so the **read and write speed is extremely fast**, and it is often used in **scenarios such as caches, message queues, distributed locks, etc.**.

Atomicity is crucial in systems that need high consistency and reliability, especially when dealing with critical operations like financial transactions or complex state changes. Each of these commands serves specific use cases: - MGET: Efficient bulk retrieval of string values - HGETALL: Complete hash inspection and data retrieval - GETDEL: One-time use tokens and atomic consume operations - GETSET: Atomic value updates with previous value tracking - GETRANGE: String manipulation and partial content retrieval String Operations SET Command The SET command sets a string value for a key: - **Syntax**: SET key value [EX seconds] [PX milliseconds] [NX XX] - **Purpose**: Sets the string value of a key, with optional expiration and conditions - **Returns**: OK if successful, nil if conditions not met - **Examples**:

It sounds quite simple, but it’s not to be overlooked that there are risk points in this process. The most common ones are network disconnection or blockage. If the network is disconnected, the master and slave databases can’t conduct command propagation, and naturally, the data of the slave database can’t be kept consistent with that of the master database. Clients may then read old data from the slave database. ヽ (*。>Д<) o ゜

Well, once the master and slave databases have completed full — replication, they will always maintain a network connection. The master database will use this connection to synchronize the subsequently received command operations to the slave database. This process is also known as command propagation based on a long — connection and can avoid the overhead of frequently establishing connections.

In the previous two articles, we have learned about AOF (Append Only File) and RDB (Redis Database). If Redis crashes, they can respectively recover data by replaying the logs and re-reading the RDB file, thus ensuring minimal data loss and enhancing reliability.

Starting from Redis 2.8, after the network is disconnected, the master and slave databases will continue synchronization by adopting the incremental replication method. questions.question: RDB vs AOF?
questions.core_answer: RDB: snapshots. AOF: every write logged. Use both. Know fsync options.
questions.deep_dive:
RDB gives point-in-time snapshots, so restart and backup flows are simple and fast, but you can lose data generated after the last snapshot. AOF appends write commands to a log, which improves durability because Redis can replay the operations after restart. The durability and cost depend on the fsync policy, so `always` is safest and slowest, while `everysec` is a common balance in production. A practical answer is that many teams use both: RDB for compact snapshots and fast recovery, AOF for better durability.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/2. Implement Redis/5.DataPersistence.md
- RDB (Redis Database): This is a snapshot of the data that is created at regular intervals according to the configuration. For example, every 3 minutes or every 10 minutes, depending on how you configure it. In this method, Redis takes a complete copy of the data in memory and saves it to a file. When a restart or crash occurs, the data is reloaded from the RDB file.

- AOF (Append only file): In this method, Redis records each command in the file as RESP. When a restart occurs, Redis reads all the RESP commands from the AOF file and executes them in memory. AOF

With this, we have completed the AOF implementation and learned how to persist data on disk. It’s worth noting that Redis uses the same approach for persistence. You can read this article to learn more about the differences between RDB and AOF.

Note that we use v.Marshal() to write the command to the file in the same RESP format that we receive. This way, when we read the file later, we can parse these RESP lines and write them back to memory. Writing the AOF All we need to do now is use NewAof in main.go and write to the AOF file with every request from the client.

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis What is Master-Slave Replication and How is it Implemented?.md
After the RDB file generated by the master server is sent and the slave server receives the RDB file, it discards all the old data and loads the RDB data into the memory. After completing the loading of the RDB file, it will reply with a confirmation message to the master server.

In the previous two articles, we have learned about AOF (Append Only File) and RDB (Redis Database). If Redis crashes, they can respectively recover data by replaying the logs and re-reading the RDB file, thus ensuring minimal data loss and enhancing reliability.

AOF and RDB ensure the former. As for the latter, what Redis does is to increase replicas, that is, store a copy of data on multiple instances simultaneously. Even if one instance fails and takes some time to recover, other instances can still provide services to the outside world without affecting business usage.

However, the write operation commands during this period are not recorded in the just-generated RDB file, and at this time, the data between the master and slave servers is inconsistent.

questions.question: Pub/Sub vs Streams?
questions.core_answer: Pub/Sub: fire-forget. Streams: persistent, consumer groups, replay.
questions.deep_dive:
Pub/Sub is good when you care about fan-out and immediacy but not message durability. If a subscriber is offline, the message is gone. That makes it fine for transient notifications, chat presence, or live UI updates. If you need replay, consumer state, acknowledgments, or durable processing, you should move to something like Redis Streams or Kafka. The interview mistake is treating Pub/Sub like a reliable work queue when it is not designed for that.

questions.question: Redis replication?
questions.core_answer: Full sync: PSYNC→RDB→buffered. Incremental: replication backlog.
questions.deep_dive:
Full sync: PSYNC→RDB→buffered. Incremental: replication backlog.

Why this matters in Redis: this topic usually appears when interviewers are checking whether you can connect design choices to reliability, latency, and operability under real load.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis What is Master-Slave Replication and How is it Implemented?.md
Starting from Redis 2.8, after the network is disconnected, the master and slave databases will continue synchronization by adopting the incremental replication method. As you can probably guess from its name, it’s different from full replication: full replication synchronizes all data, while incremental replication only synchronizes the commands received by the master database during the network disconnection period to the slave database.

When the master and slave servers synchronize for the first time, full replication is adopted. At this time, there are two time-consuming aspects for the master server, namely generating the RDB file and transmitting the RDB file. In order to avoid too many slave servers conducting full replication with the master server, a part of the slave servers can be upgraded to “secondary master servers” so that they also have their own slave servers. Through this way, the pressure on the master server can be shared.

There are three modes of master-slave replication: full replication, command propagation based on long connections, and incremental replication.

If the network is disconnected, incremental replication will come into play, which is closely related to the size of the parameter repl_backlog_size. If it is configured too small, when the network of the master and slave servers is restored, it may happen that the data that the "slave server" wants to read has already been overwritten. Then, this will lead to the master server adopting the full replication method. Therefore, in order to avoid the frequent occurrence of this situation, the value of this parameter should be increased to reduce the probability of full synchronization after the master and slave servers are disconnected.

questions.question: Production metrics?
questions.core_answer: Memory/RSS/fragmentation, ops/sec, hits/misses, slow commands, replica lag.
questions.deep_dive:
I would start with memory usage, peak memory, RSS, and any signal that memory is approaching `maxmemory`, because eviction or fragmentation problems can change behavior quickly. Then I would watch ops per second, keyspace hits versus misses, slow commands, blocked clients, rejected connections, and replication lag or replica health. The point is to cover the main failure modes: memory pressure, bad cache efficiency, client pressure, and replication health. For debugging, I would pair metrics with `INFO`, `SLOWLOG`, `CLIENT LIST`, and the Redis exporter in Prometheus.

questions.question: How does Redis replica first sync work from `PSYNC` to `FULLRESYNC`?
questions.core_answer: A new replica connects with `PSYNC`; on first sync the master replies `FULLRESYNC`, creates an RDB snapshot, sends it, buffers new writes, then replays those buffered writes so the replica catches up.
questions.deep_dive:
A new replica uses `replicaof` and then starts synchronization with `PSYNC`. For the first sync, the master responds with `FULLRESYNC`, creates an RDB snapshot, sends it to the replica, and buffers writes that happen during that transfer. After the replica loads the RDB, the master replays the buffered writes so both sides converge. That means the first sync is really a three-part flow: handshake, bulk snapshot transfer, and buffered command catch-up.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis What is Master-Slave Replication and How is it Implemented?.md
After the connection between the master and slave databases is restored, the slave database will first send the psync command to the master database and send its current slave_repl_offset to the master database. Then the master database will judge the difference between its own master_repl_offset and slave_repl_offset.

When the master and slave servers synchronize for the first time, full replication is adopted. At this time, there are two time-consuming aspects for the master server, namely generating the RDB file and transmitting the RDB file. In order to avoid too many slave servers conducting full replication with the master server, a part of the slave servers can be upgraded to “secondary master servers” so that they also have their own slave servers. Through this way, the pressure on the master server can be shared.

- During the period when the master server generates the RDB file; - During the period when the master server sends the RDB file to the slave server; - During the period when the ‘slave server’ loads the RDB file;

By analyzing the process of the first data synchronization between the master and slave databases, you can see that in a full replication, for the master database, there are two time-consuming operations to be completed: generating the RDB file and transmitting the RDB file.

questions.question: Why does `repl-backlog-size` matter for avoiding expensive resyncs?
questions.core_answer: Redis keeps recent writes in the replication backlog. If a replica reconnects before its missing offset is overwritten, it can do a partial resync; if not, Redis must send a full snapshot again.
questions.deep_dive:
Incremental replication is Redis's way of catching a replica up after a temporary disconnect without redoing a full sync. The master stores recent write history in `repl_backlog_buffer`, which is a circular buffer. When the replica reconnects, it reports its replication offset and the master sends only the missing operations if they still exist in the backlog. If the backlog is too small and the needed entries were overwritten, Redis has to fall back to a full resync, which is much more expensive. A good answer includes sizing the backlog based on reconnect time and average write volume.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis What is Master-Slave Replication and How is it Implemented?.md
Starting from Redis 2.8, after the network is disconnected, the master and slave databases will continue synchronization by adopting the incremental replication method. As you can probably guess from its name, it’s different from full replication: full replication synchronizes all data, while incremental replication only synchronizes the commands received by the master database during the network disconnection period to the slave database.

However, there’s one point that needs attention! The default size of the repl_backlog_buffer buffer is 1M. And since the repl_backlog_buffer is a circular buffer, after the buffer is full, the master database will continue to write, and at this time, the previously written operations will be overwritten. If the reading speed of the slave database is relatively slow, it may lead to the situation where the operations that the slave database hasn't read yet are overwritten by the new operations written by the master database, which will result in data inconsistency between the master and slave databases.

If the network is disconnected, incremental replication will come into play, which is closely related to the size of the parameter repl_backlog_size. If it is configured too small, when the network of the master and slave servers is restored, it may happen that the data that the "slave server" wants to read has already been overwritten. Then, this will lead to the master server adopting the full replication method. Therefore, in order to avoid the frequent occurrence of this situation, the value of this parameter should be increased to reduce the probability of full synchronization after the master and slave servers are disconnected.
notes: Interview framing: Size backlog from disconnect window times write rate.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/5. Apache Kafka/Apache Kafka® Tiered Storage in Depth - How Writes and Metadata Flow.md
- The same remote segment and topic-partition IDs - The (updated) state of the segment - e.g COPY_FINISHED - The plugin-specific custom metadata. With the Aiven plugin, this consists of the: - The blob object’s key. It’s in the format of **$(topic_name)-$(topic_uuid)/$(partition)/$(000+start_offset length=20)-$(remote_segment_uuid)** - The object prefix (the key.prefix config which denotes a general prefix string for all keys) - The size of the remote blob (this is relevant when encryption/compression changes it)

As with any materialization process, the ordering matters! We can’t afford to have an update record be read before a general record. To ensure ordering, Kafka deterministically places metadata records of user topic partitions in the same metadata topic partition.

questions.question: Sidecar pattern?
questions.core_answer: Helper process for cross-cutting concerns. Foundation of service mesh.
questions.deep_dive:
The sidecar pattern moves cross-cutting communication concerns out of the app and into a co-located proxy or helper process. That proxy can handle protocol upgrades, mTLS, tracing, retries, discovery, or logging without every service embedding that logic in its own language runtime. This is powerful in polyglot environments because the application only talks to localhost using a simple contract while the sidecar handles the complex network behavior. The trade-off is more moving parts, more resource overhead, and sometimes harder debugging.

questions.question: What are the main design concerns in request-response systems?
questions.core_answer: Framing, serialization cost, network latency, timeouts, retries, payload size, and what happens when work is slow or partial. Good protocols make message boundaries and failure behavior explicit.
questions.deep_dive:
The core concerns are framing, serialization cost, network latency, server-side processing cost, and what happens when requests are large or long-running. Over TCP, request boundaries are not magic, so the protocol must define them clearly. Serialization choices like JSON versus protobuf affect latency, payload size, and developer ergonomics. For large uploads, chunking is often better than single-shot requests because you gain resumability, finer-grained retries, and smaller memory pressure.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Udemy/Fundamentals of Backend Communications and Protocols/Section 2 Backend Communication Design Patterns/7 Request Response.md

- **Parsing cost**: large JSON/XML can be expensive to parse. - **Serialization cost**: serializing complex objects can be expensive. - **Network cost**: latency and throughput matter. Packets may be reordered. - **Server-side assembly**: chunked uploads require bookkeeping and storage overhead. - **Timeouts & disconnects**: long synchronous requests risk client disconnects and lost work. - **Head-of-line blocking** and pipeline issues — do not rely on packet order for correctness.

- Request/response is elegant & ubiquitous, but not always the best fit. - Parsing and framing costs are real — choose serialization carefully. - For large or long-running tasks, decouple with queues or push mechanisms. - Understand the _end-to-end timeline_ — every micro-stage contributes to latency.

questions.question: How do you explain synchronous vs asynchronous workloads cleanly in an interview?
questions.core_answer: Synchronous means the caller waits and progress is blocked. Asynchronous means work is handed off and the caller can continue, which is why async models help most for I/O-bound systems.
questions.deep_dive:
The simplest mental model is whether the caller can do useful work while waiting. In synchronous execution, the caller waits and progress is blocked. In asynchronous execution, the caller hands work off and continues, receiving the result later through a callback, event, future, or queue. This matters at the language level and at the system-design level. Good candidates connect it to blocking I/O, event loops, thread utilization, and why async communication usually improves throughput for I/O-bound systems.

- The caller **does not wait** - The caller can **continue doing other work** - The result is delivered **later** (callback, promise, event, etc.) Intuition

questions.question: What are the trade-offs of server push systems?
questions.core_answer: Push gives low-latency delivery, but it also requires many live connections, online clients, and careful back-pressure. It trades repeated polling for connection-management complexity.
questions.deep_dive:
Push is great for low-latency delivery because the server can send updates the moment an event happens. But it also means the client must be online, the system must maintain many live connections, and the server can overwhelm clients if back-pressure is not handled well. Large fan-out systems often need intermediaries such as mobile push providers or brokered architectures instead of naive direct push from the core service. In other words, push reduces polling delay but increases connection management complexity.

- Over TCP a _stream_ of bytes is delivered. The server must detect where one request ends and the next begins. - Protocols and headers (e.g., HTTP Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding) define the boundary. - **Parsing cost** matters (e.g., XML costly; JSON cheaper; protobuf fastest for some cases).

- **Request/Response** = the simplest and most common backend communication pattern. - **Client** sends a _request_. - **Server** parses and processes the request, then sends a _response_. - Both sides must **agree on the message structure** (protocol + serialization).

- Parsing, deserializing, processing and serializing responses all cost CPU/time. - The **boundary** (where a request starts/ends) is non-trivial — especially over TCP (stream). - Designing request/response effectively influences performance, reliability, and UX.

questions.question: DTOs vs entities?
questions.core_answer: Shape API, exclude sensitive fields, separation of concerns.
questions.deep_dive:
DTOs let you shape an API contract intentionally instead of leaking internal entity structure. That helps with security because you can exclude fields like passwords, internal IDs, or audit details. It also helps performance because you can flatten or aggregate data to reduce extra calls and tailor payloads to the client use case. A strong answer mentions contract stability, versioning, and separation of persistence concerns from API concerns.

questions.question: Exception handling?
questions.core_answer: @ControllerAdvice. Consistent error envelope. Don't leak stack traces.
questions.deep_dive:
You want a consistent error envelope across the API, not random stack traces or framework defaults leaking into responses. `@ControllerAdvice` gives you a central place to translate domain exceptions and unexpected exceptions into structured HTTP responses with the right status codes. Specific handlers should cover known cases like not found or validation failures, and a fallback handler should catch unhandled exceptions and map them to a controlled 500 response. The design goal is consistency, observability, and not exposing internals accidentally.

questions.question: What problems is Spring Cloud trying to solve in a microservices platform?
questions.core_answer: It standardizes repeated platform concerns like service discovery, centralized config, gateway routing, circuit breaking, clients, and observability. Without it, every service reinvents infrastructure differently.
questions.deep_dive:
Spring Cloud packages the common infrastructure patterns that show up once you stop building a single service and start building a service ecosystem. That includes service discovery, centralized configuration, circuit breaking, API gateways, declarative clients, tracing, and event-driven communication. Without those patterns, each service ends up hardcoding URLs, managing its own configs, and handling failures inconsistently. Spring Cloud is valuable less because it is magical and more because it standardizes patterns teams would otherwise implement badly or differently.

questions.question: How do Eureka, Config Server, Gateway, and Circuit Breakers fit together?
questions.core_answer: Eureka tracks instances, Config Server centralizes settings, Gateway routes and secures entry traffic, and circuit breakers stop cascading failures. Together they make a service fleet operable instead of just deployed.
questions.deep_dive:
Eureka is the registry that tracks service instances so callers do not hardcode hostnames. Config Server centralizes configuration, often from Git, so settings can be managed consistently across services and environments. The API Gateway is the entry point that routes requests, often with load balancing and security controls. Circuit Breakers keep cascading failures under control by failing fast and returning fallbacks when downstream services are unhealthy. Together, they turn a collection of services into an operable platform rather than a pile of apps.

questions.question: ModelMapper vs MapStruct: how would you choose?
questions.core_answer: ModelMapper is quick to wire and fine for small apps. MapStruct generates compile-time mapping code, so it is usually better for large systems that want performance, type safety, and early failure.
questions.deep_dive:
ModelMapper is convenient for quick setup and convention-based runtime mapping, which is useful in smaller projects or prototypes. MapStruct generates mapping code at compile time, so it gives better performance, stronger type safety, and earlier failure if mappings break. For enterprise services with many mappings and strict correctness needs, I would usually pick MapStruct. If the problem is tiny and speed of setup matters more than optimization, ModelMapper is acceptable.

questions.question: Why customize validation error responses instead of returning framework defaults?
questions.core_answer: Default validation payloads are noisy and unstable. A clean field-to-message response makes client handling easier and keeps invalid input as a clear `400 Bad Request` contract.
questions.deep_dive:
Default validation errors are often noisy and not client-friendly. A customized validation handler can return a clean field-to-message map so the client knows exactly what failed and why. That also makes front-end handling simpler and produces a more stable contract for consumers. The key detail is that validation failures should normally be `400 Bad Request`, not `500 Internal Server Error`, because the client sent invalid data rather than the server breaking.

Exception Handling in Spring Boot REST APIs Introduction - Welcome back to the lectures. - In this section, we will explore exception handling in Spring Boot REST APIs. - Handling exceptions and returning custom error responses to clients is a best practice in enterprise applications. Overview of Spring Boot Error Handling - Our Spring Boot application consists of different layers: - **Controller Layer**: Handles incoming requests. - **Service Layer**: Contains request validation and business logic. - **Repository Layer**: Manages data-related logic. Request Flow 1. A client sends a request to the **Controller Layer**. 2. The controller processes the request and forwards it to the **Service Layer**. 3. The service layer validates the request. If an error occurs during validation, an exception is thrown. 4. Spring Boot's default error handling catches the exception and creates a custom error response in JSON format, which is sent back to the client. Default Error Response - The default error response from Spring Boot includes: - timestamp - status - error - path - Example of a default error response:

Custom Error Response - While the default error response is useful, clients may require a different format. - In real-time projects, we need to customize the error response to meet client expectations. - We will use the following format for our custom error response: - timestamp - message - path - error code Example Scenario - Let's consider a scenario where we call the "Get User by ID" API. - If we pass a user ID that does not exist in the database (e.g., ID 10), the default error response will return a 500 status code. - This is incorrect; the response should indicate a 404 status code with a message like "Resource Not Found."

questions.question: Music streaming service?
questions.core_answer: CDN audio, metadata service, search (ES), recommendations. Adaptive bitrate.
questions.deep_dive:
I would separate metadata from the audio objects. Song metadata, user data, playlists, and playback state belong in operational databases optimized for queries and updates, while the audio files themselves belong in object storage because they are large, immutable blobs. Search and discovery can sit on top of a search service, and actual playback should lean heavily on CDN distribution because hot songs create network and bandwidth bottlenecks long before they create CPU bottlenecks. A strong answer also covers caching, chunked streaming, regional replication, and the difference between metadata traffic and audio traffic.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Problems/1. Design Spotify.md
- The database for a music streaming service like Spotify can be split into two separate databases: a song audio database and a metadata database, to handle different types of data 13:20.

- Amazon S3 is a good choice for the song audio database because it scales linearly and can handle large amounts of data, while Amazon RDS is a good choice for the metadata database because it can handle queries and updates 15:43.

- The metadata database would store information such as song ID, song name, artist, genre, and links to album covers and audio files, and would need to be able to handle updates, such as when a user pauses a song and wants to resume playing it later 17:20.

- The song audio database would be optimized for read-heavy access patterns, with the ability to stream data, while the metadata database would need to handle both reads and writes, as well as queries to find specific data 16:04.

questions.question: Subscribe-and-save?
questions.core_answer: Subscription + scheduler + order + payment + notifications. Edge cases: payment failures, inventory.
questions.deep_dive:
The hard parts are not CRUD; they are recurring scheduling, payment retries, stock availability, price changes, pause or skip flows, and user communication before the next charge. You need a strong source of truth for subscription state, a scheduler or event system that generates future orders, and careful handling of payment and inventory failure paths. The system also needs strong consistency around pause, cancel, and next-order-date updates because duplicate or stale state can create bad charges or bad user experiences. Good candidates also talk about idempotency, retries with backoff, and notifying users when products or prices change.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/3. Mastering Data Consistency Across Microservices.md
- Microservices operate with independent databases, making data consistency challenging. However, ensuring consistency is crucial for reliability, user trust, and preventing financial or operational errors. - Different types of consistency models can be explored while designing the services. - Strong consistency ensures immediate accuracy but impacts performance. - Eventual consistency allows temporary inconsistencies but improves scalability. - Causal consistency maintains event order across services. - Read-your-writes consistency ensures users see their updates immediately. - Multiple strategies can be used to facilitate data consistency across services. - Synchronous communication provides strong consistency but can cause bottlenecks. - Asynchronous messaging improves scalability but requires handling eventual consistency. - Choreography and Orchestration ensure consistency by handling distributed transactions with compensating actions. - An event-driven architecture enables eventual consistency through event sourcing and CQRS. - Change Data Capture (CDC) streams database changes to ensure real-time consistency.

- The Orchestrator receives an order request. - It calls the Payment Service to process the payment. - If successful, it calls the Shipping Service to initiate delivery. - If the inventory update fails, the orchestrator calls the Payment Service to refund the transaction. It also calls the Order Service to mark the order as “CANCELLED”.

questions.question: Back-of-envelope estimation?
questions.core_answer: Round assumptions, order of magnitude. Users → QPS → storage → bandwidth.
questions.deep_dive:
Start with a few explicit assumptions, keep the math round, and focus on the order of magnitude. For example, estimate user counts, active rates, requests per user, object size, and retention period, then turn those into QPS, storage, and bandwidth. The goal is not perfect arithmetic; it is to show that you can reason about whether the design needs a single database, sharding, a CDN, or offline processing. If your assumptions are reasonable and your architecture changes logically based on them, the estimation is doing its job.

- Every broker tiers its user partition segments and indices to a remote store - The tiering happens asynchronously and only once certain requirements are fulfilled (closed segment, LSO, indices present, etc) - The state of this tiering is kept in an internal topic named **remote_log_metadata**. - Before and after tiering, the broker writes the state of the tiering and plugin-specific metadata to the appropriate **remote_log_metadata** partitions. - The Aiven plugin stores the data in three different blobs in object storage: 1. Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/1. A Comprehensive Guide to Database Sharding.md
Range-based sharding splits up the data by sorting the values in one or more columns in lexicographic order and using ranges of such values. For example, you might divide a user database based on user ID ranges or a product database based on price, etc.

The advantage of range-based sharding is that it is simple. The application can quickly determine which shard to write to or read from based on the value of the sharding key. It also makes range queries efficient. You know exactly which shard to query if you need all users with IDs between 1,500,000 and 1,800,000. To make range scans fast, each shard is generally stored in sorted order on the disk.

This mechanism keeps related data together on a single physical shard. For example, in a social media application, you might shard based on user ID, but ensure that a user's posts, comments, and profile information all end up on the same shard.

1. _Immutability_. The shard key should be immutable. If the shard key value changes, it might be necessary to move the data to another shard, which is costly. Using a user's email address as a shard key might seem reasonable, but not if users can change their email addresses.

questions.question: Avoid hotspots?
questions.core_answer: Better partition key, consistent hashing, CDN, coalescing, replication.
questions.deep_dive:
I would first identify what the hotspot actually is: data skew, request skew, a hot key, a hot shard, a hot cache item, or a hot region. Then I would choose the mitigation that matches the failure mode: better partition keys, consistent hashing, CDN or edge caching, per-key rate limiting, request coalescing, replication, or workload-aware load balancing. The important point is that "just add more servers" often does not fix hotspots if all traffic still lands on the same logical unit.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Problems/1. Design Spotify.md
- Implementing a more intelligent load balancing system, rather than a typical round-robin approach, would allow for more efficient distribution of requests and better overall system performance 37:19. Drill down - cache 37:30

- Replicating data is not only for availability and downtime but also for placing replicas closer to users, which would require a geo-aware strategy of data placement and replication to reduce latency and improve performance 38:21.

- The total audio data would be around 500 terabytes or half a petabyte, and with 3x replication, the total raw audio data would be approximately one and a half petabytes 07:05.

- Caching is an important point in this design, as it helps with the bottleneck of hot songs, and technologies like CloudFront, a Content Delivery Network, can be used to achieve this 31:16.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/1. A Comprehensive Guide to Database Sharding.md
With a shard key, you can quickly find and change data by routing operations to the correct database. A group of data that have the same shard key is known as a logical shard. Multiple logical shards can be hosted in the same database node, known as a physical shard. **Range-based sharding**

3. _Frequency._ The frequency of a shard key represents how often a particular shard key value appears in the dataset. If a significant portion of your entries contains only a subset of the possible shard key values, the corresponding shards become hotspots. Shards rebalancing

1. _Immutability_. The shard key should be immutable. If the shard key value changes, it might be necessary to move the data to another shard, which is costly. Using a user's email address as a shard key might seem reasonable, but not if users can change their email addresses.

2. _Cardinality_. The number of unique values a shard key can have determines the maximum number of shards that can be created. If you choose the sex of a person as a shard key, you're limited to only two shards, which doesn't give much benefit in terms of scalability. Choosing a shard key with high cardinality also allows for an even distribution of data across a larger number of shards.

questions.core_answer: Scheduling, retries, payment failures, inventory changes, pause or skip flows, price changes, and customer notifications. The hard part is getting recurring state transitions and failure handling right.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/3. Mastering Data Consistency Across Microservices.md
- **Increased Latency:** If a service takes longer to respond, the entire request chain is delayed. - **Reduced Availability:** If one service is down, dependent services cannot proceed. This can result in a system-wide failure. - **Tight Coupling:** Services become interdependent, making deployments and changes more complex.

- Microservices operate with independent databases, making data consistency challenging. However, ensuring consistency is crucial for reliability, user trust, and preventing financial or operational errors. - Different types of consistency models can be explored while designing the services. - Strong consistency ensures immediate accuracy but impacts performance. - Eventual consistency allows temporary inconsistencies but improves scalability. - Causal consistency maintains event order across services. - Read-your-writes consistency ensures users see their updates immediately. - Multiple strategies can be used to facilitate data consistency across services. - Synchronous communication provides strong consistency but can cause bottlenecks. - Asynchronous messaging improves scalability but requires handling eventual consistency. - Choreography and Orchestration ensure consistency by handling distributed transactions with compensating actions. - An event-driven architecture enables eventual consistency through event sourcing and CQRS. - Change Data Capture (CDC) streams database changes to ensure real-time consistency.

In CDC, the database maintains a change log (for example, MySQL binlog or PostgreSQL WAL). A CDC tool like Debezium monitors the logs and streams changes to other services. This allows microservices to stay eventually consistent by processing changes in near real-time.

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/1. A Comprehensive Guide to Database Sharding.md
Additionally, sharding makes also the overall system more available. If one shard goes down, the others can continue to operate, reducing the risk of complete system failure. Disadvantages of sharding

The alternative is dynamic sharding, where the system can create, split, or merge shards on demand. You typically start with a small number of shards and let the system adjust as data volume changes.

While sharding can make a database much more scalable, faster, and available, it is not a free lunch since it makes the system design more complicated.

To work around that, data needs to be split into pieces called shards, small enough to fit into individual nodes. As an additional benefit, the system's capacity for handling requests also increases since the load of accessing the data is spread over more nodes.

questions.question: How do you compare synchronous API chains with event-driven workflows?
questions.core_answer: Sync flows are simpler to reason about but add coupling, latency, and cascading-failure risk. Event-driven flows improve decoupling and throughput, but they add retries, eventual consistency, ordering, and harder debugging.
questions.deep_dive:
Synchronous chains are simpler to reason about because failures are immediate and control flow is explicit, but they raise latency, coupling, and cascading-failure risk. Event-driven workflows improve decoupling and throughput, and they tolerate downstream outages better because work can sit in a broker. But they also introduce eventual consistency, retries, ordering concerns, and more complicated debugging. The best answer is usually not ideological; it is to use synchronous paths where the user needs an immediate result and asynchronous flows where durability and decoupling matter more than instant completion.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/3. Mastering Data Consistency Across Microservices.md

sections.name: Elasticsearch
sections.summary: Query execution, profiling, wildcard behavior, and debugging search latency at shard level.

questions.question: Search query execution?
questions.core_answer: Query phase (scatter, get IDs) → Fetch phase (get documents). BM25.
questions.deep_dive:
Elasticsearch typically executes a search in two main phases: query and fetch. In the query phase, the coordinating node sends the query to all relevant shards, and each shard returns lightweight matches such as document IDs and scores. The coordinating node merges those shard-level results into a globally ranked list. In the fetch phase, Elasticsearch asks the relevant shards for the full document contents of only the top results. This design keeps the first phase cheap and avoids moving large payloads across the network until Elasticsearch knows which hits actually matter.

What strong candidates mention: coordinating node, shard-local execution, top-N merge, and why fetch is separated from query.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Elasticsearch/Notes.md
Here’s a breakdown of each phase: 1. Query Phase This is the first part of the search process. - What it does: The node that receives your search request (the coordinating node) forwards the query to every shard in the index. Each shard executes the query locally on its own set of data. - What it returns: Each shard creates a lightweight list of results containing only the document IDs and their relevance scores (_score). It does not load the full content of the documents yet. These small lists are sent back to the coordinating node. - Goal: The main goal is to identify which documents match the query and how well they match, without the overhead of moving large amounts of data across the network. The coordinating node merges the lists from all shards to create one final, globally sorted list of document IDs. A search_query entry in your slow logs means that this initial identification and scoring process was slow on a particular shard. This is often caused by expensive query types like leading wildcards, complex aggregations, or scripts. 2. Fetch Phase
notes: Interview framing: Query-then-fetch.
For latency questions, identify phase-level timing first so optimization targets the real bottleneck.
Differentiate query-phase cost from fetch-phase cost before selecting fixes.
Use profile and rewrite output to prove where latency originates.
Pair text relevance with mapping/index strategy to keep latency predictable.

The first method takes an approximate nearest neighbor approach—it uses one of several algorithms to return the approximate k-nearest neighbors to a query vector. questions.question: N-grams vs wildcards?
questions.core_answer: N-grams: index-time work. Wildcards: query-time scan. N-grams = predictable latency.
questions.deep_dive:
Leading wildcard queries force the engine to rewrite the pattern into an automaton and scan large parts of the term dictionary at query time. That is expensive, hard to cache well, and gets worse as the corpus grows. N-grams and `search_as_you_type` move that cost to index time by precomputing searchable fragments. At query time, the search becomes a combination of ordinary term lookups instead of a wide dictionary scan. The trade-off is more index size and indexing overhead, but the query latency is usually far more predictable.

questions.question: Why do Elasticsearch slow logs appear at the shard level instead of the cluster level?
questions.core_answer: The data node doing shard work emits them, not the coordinating node. That matters because one bad shard often dominates latency, so shard logs expose the real bottleneck faster.
questions.deep_dive:
Slow logs are emitted by the data nodes that actually execute the shard work, not by the coordinating node that accepted the client request. That matters because search latency is often caused by one or two bad shards rather than the entire cluster being uniformly slow. A slow `search_query` log means the matching and scoring work was expensive on that shard. A slow `search_fetch` log usually points to expensive document retrieval, large `_source` payloads, highlighting, or poor I/O. If you understand that distinction, you know where to start debugging instead of treating the cluster as a black box.

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis What is Master-Slave Replication and How is it Implemented?.md
Starting from Redis 2.8, after the network is disconnected, the master and slave databases will continue synchronization by adopting the incremental replication method. As you can probably guess from its name, it’s different from full replication: full replication synchronizes all data, while incremental replication only synchronizes the commands received by the master database during the network disconnection period to the slave database.

When the master and slave servers synchronize for the first time, full replication is adopted. At this time, there are two time-consuming aspects for the master server, namely generating the RDB file and transmitting the RDB file. In order to avoid too many slave servers conducting full replication with the master server, a part of the slave servers can be upgraded to “secondary master servers” so that they also have their own slave servers. Through this way, the pressure on the master server can be shared.

There are three modes of master-slave replication: full replication, command propagation based on long connections, and incremental replication.

- runID: Each Redis server will automatically generate a random ID when it starts up to uniquely identify itself. When the slave server synchronizes with the master server for the first time, since it doesn't know the runID of the master server, it will set it to "?". - offset: It represents the replication progress. When synchronizing for the first time, its value is -1.

questions.question: What risks matter in a large caching layer beyond just cache misses?
questions.core_answer: Hot keys, stampedes, uneven routing, stale data, proxy bottlenecks, and connection storms. Real cache design is about blast radius control, not just hit ratio.
questions.deep_dive:
Common risks include hot keys, uneven routing, connection storms, stampedes after expiry, stale data, and proxy or network bottlenecks even when cache servers themselves are healthy. Another risk is building too much application logic into the cache layer until it becomes hard to debug or change safely. In interviews, it helps to talk about traffic shaping, failover, request coalescing, layered caching, and observability instead of treating cache as a simple key-value box.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Meghacache/Memcached as proxy.md
1. **Script Execution**: It compiles and runs Lua code that can interact with cache operations. 2. **Extension Mechanism**: It allows developers to customize Memcached's behavior beyond its built-in commands. 3. **Request Interception**: In proxy scenarios, the Lua engine can intercept incoming requests, analyze them, and determine where to route them. 4. **Custom Logic**: It enables implementation of custom caching policies, routing rules, and data transformations.

4. Replication Support: - The proxy can be configured for cache replication scenarios - It supports "blind copying" of sets and deletes to multiple pools - This is a best-effort system rather than strong synchronization - Useful for scenarios like: - Minimizing impact of dead cache servers - Replicating specific subsets of cache data - Maintaining copies across different availability zones

2. Pool Management: - The proxy operates in terms of "pools" of servers rather than individual backends - Each pool can contain multiple backend Memcached servers - Keys are typically hashed and mapped to specific servers within a pool - This design allows for efficient memory utilization across the cache cluster

This architecture allows for flexible deployment scenarios where you can: - Scale your cache horizontally - Implement different routing strategies - Handle failover scenarios - Manage cache replication - Provide TLS support - Optimize for specific use cases

Source: Technical/Redis/Redis What is Master-Slave Replication and How is it Implemented?.md
If the network is disconnected, incremental replication will come into play, which is closely related to the size of the parameter repl_backlog_size. If it is configured too small, when the network of the master and slave servers is restored, it may happen that the data that the "slave server" wants to read has already been overwritten. Then, this will lead to the master server adopting the full replication method. Therefore, in order to avoid the frequent occurrence of this situation, the value of this parameter should be increased to reduce the probability of full synchronization after the master and slave servers are disconnected.

It sounds quite simple, but it’s not to be overlooked that there are risk points in this process. The most common ones are network disconnection or blockage. If the network is disconnected, the master and slave databases can’t conduct command propagation, and naturally, the data of the slave database can’t be kept consistent with that of the master database. Clients may then read old data from the slave database. ヽ (*。>Д<) o ゜

After the first synchronization is completed, the master and slave servers will maintain a long connection. After receiving write operation commands, the master server will propagate the write commands to the slave server through this connection to ensure the data consistency between the master and slave servers.

After the RDB file generated by the master server is sent and the slave server receives the RDB file, it discards all the old data and loads the RDB data into the memory. After completing the loading of the RDB file, it will reply with a confirmation message to the master server.

A **framework** is typically a set of tools and libraries that developers use to simplify coding, enforce structure, and provide common features like authentication, logging, and more. Examples of frameworks include **Spring Boot** for Java or **Express.js** for Node.js.

1. **Spring Boot (Java)**: One of the most popular frameworks for building microservices, Spring Boot simplifies the development process by offering auto-configuration, embedded servers, and RESTful APIs. 2. **Node.js with Express**: A lightweight framework that enables developers to build microservices using JavaScript and Node.js. 3. **.NET Core**: A cross-platform framework from Microsoft that provides support for building microservices with C#. 4. **Django (Python)**: A high-level Python framework that can be used to develop microservices by utilizing its RESTful API support. Benefits of Microservices Architecture 1. **Scalability**

With microservices, you can scale individual services based on demand. For example, if one service experiences higher traffic than others, you can scale that service independently without affecting the rest of the application. 2. **Faster Development**

Microservices architecture promotes fault tolerance. If one service fails, it doesn’t bring down the entire application, as other services can continue running independently. 5. **Ease of Deployment**

Source: Technical/System Design/Distributed Concepts/5. Apache Kafka/Apache Kafka® Tiered Storage in Depth - How Writes and Metadata Flow.md
- **Tiered Storage** - the feature that KIP-405 introduces. - **External Store** - the secondary cold storage system to which the data gets tiered. This is most commonly a cloud object store like S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Store. - **Segment**- a regular log file in Kafka that stores the partition’s data. - **Chunk** - one small part of a segment - a subset of its data. (e.g 4 MiB out of the 1 GiB segment). It is a concept that is specific and internal to Aiven’s Tiered Storage plugin. Tiered Storage Writes

1. The broker decides it’ll tier a local segment. It creates a unique UUID for the **remote** log segment. It creates a metadata record with a state of COPY_STARTED and produces it durably to the internal Kafka topic. 2. It uploads the data via the plugin. The plugin returns a set of custom metadata specific to the plugin (KIP-917). 3. A new record referring to the same remote segment UUID, this time with an updated COPY_FINISHED state, is persisted in the Kafka topic. It also contains the plugin metadata.

At any one time, there is only one so-called “active” segment. This is the open file that the latest data is appended to. After a configurable size/time threshold passes, the segment gets “closed”, and a new active one is created. When to Upload

- Network bandwidth - the plugin sends the data to the external storage over the wire. - Disk bandwidth - the plugin needs to read the data it’s about to tier from disk. - CPU time - compressing and encrypting data can take up CPU, but even reading for disk and uploading to the external storage takes CPU, because it is not zero copy.

Range-based sharding splits up the data by sorting the values in one or more columns in lexicographic order and using ranges of such values. For example, you might divide a user database based on user ID ranges or a product database based on price, etc.

It also makes range queries efficient. You know exactly which shard to query if you need all users with IDs between 1,500,000 and 1,800,000. To make range scans fast, each shard is generally stored in sorted order on the disk.

questions.question: Exact k-NN vs ANN?
questions.core_answer: Exact: full scan, accurate. ANN: HNSW/IVF, faster, some recall loss.
questions.deep_dive:
Exact k-NN compares the query vector against the full candidate set, which gives the most accurate result but becomes expensive at scale. Approximate nearest-neighbor search uses structures like HNSW graphs or IVF clusters to reduce the search space and improve latency, usually accepting some recall loss. The practical trade-off is accuracy versus latency and cost. For small filtered candidate sets, exact methods are often fine; for large-scale semantic search, ANN is usually the only realistic option.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Artificial Intelligence/Vector Search/Opensearch/Opensearch Vector Search Notes.md
The simple way to find similar vectors is to use k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) algorithms, which compute the distance between a query vector and the other vectors in the vector database. As we mentioned earlier, the score script k-NN and painless extensions search methods use the exact k-NN algorithms under the hood. However, in the case of extremely large datasets with high dimensionality, this creates a scaling problem that reduces the efficiency of the search. Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search methods can overcome this by employing tools that restructure indexes more efficiently and reduce the dimensionality of searchable vectors. There are different ANN search algorithms; for example, locality sensitive hashing, tree-based, cluster-based, and graph-based. OpenSearch implements two ANN algorithms: Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds (HNSW) and Inverted File System (IVF). For a more detailed explanation of how the HNSW and IVF algorithms work in OpenSearch, see blog post “Choose the k-NN algorithm for your billion-scale use case with OpenSearch”. questions.question: Semantic search over slow logs?
questions.core_answer: Ingest → structured fields → summaries → embeddings → OpenSearch with vectors + metadata.
questions.deep_dive:
First, ingest raw logs and enrich them with structured fields such as took time, index, wildcard usage, aggregation depth, scripts, and duplicate fingerprints. Then generate a plain-English summary of the query characteristics and produce embeddings for the summary and possibly the raw text. Index both structured fields and vectors into OpenSearch so you can do filtered keyword search, semantic search, or a hybrid of both. This design is powerful because engineers often remember the problem semantically, like "leading wildcard slow query," rather than the exact raw DSL.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Artificial Intelligence/Vector Search/Opensearch/SafeSearch Opensearch.md
**3. Opensearch Vector Search** We are leveraging the vector search capability of OpenSearch for storing, indexing, and searching the enriched slow log data. It uses the msmarco-distilbert-base-tas-b model from Hugging Face (Sentence-Transformers) with a vector dimension of 768. An ingest pipeline (slowlog-embedding-pipeline) automatically generates vector embeddings for both the encrypted raw log (log_vector) and the human-readable summary (summary_vector) during document ingestion. All data is indexed in a k-NN enabled index (slowlogs-search-index), and a Python script is used to efficiently bulk-upload the processed JSON documents to OpenSearch.

This document outlines the architecture and usage of Vector Search for Elasticsearch Slow Logs. The system is designed to ingest raw JSON-based slow logs, perform structural and performance analysis, and index the enriched data into OpenSearch. By leveraging a sentence-transformer model for vector embeddings, the platform enables engineers to search and troubleshoot complex performance issues using natural language queries.

As part of monitoring and maintaining large-scale Elasticsearch clusters, all slow logs (for both search and indexing) are captured and stored. To make searching and analyzing these logs effective, this project ingests the data into a dedicated OpenSearch cluster and creates vector embeddings for key fields like the raw log text and a generated summary.

A crucial part of this step is generating a **human-readable summary**. This summary explicitly states the log's characteristics in plain English (e.g., "This is a high-latency search query with a leading wildcard that hit 5 shards.") to make the summary_vector highly effective for natural language search.

When you use OpenSearch Service as a vector database, you can take advantage of the service’s features like usability, scalability, availability, interoperability, and security. You can also combine OpenSearch text search and vector search capabilities to search documents with keyword and semantic similarity. You can also use other fields in the index to filter documents to improve relevance. For advanced users, you can use a hybrid scoring model to combine OpenSearch’s text-based relevance score, computed with the Okapi BM25 function and its vector search score to improve the ranking of your search results. questions.question: AI agents vs RAG?
questions.core_answer: RAG: retrieves context. Agents: multi-step actions + tools + iteration.
questions.deep_dive:
RAG is mainly about retrieving external context and feeding it into the model so the response is grounded in better information. Agentic systems go further by letting the model plan multi-step actions, choose tools, observe outputs, and continue iterating until the task is done. In other words, RAG expands memory, while agents expand capability. Agents are more powerful but also riskier because mistakes compound across steps and tools can cause real side effects.

questions.question: Hybrid search?
questions.core_answer: BM25 lexical + vector semantic + metadata filters. Blend or rerank.
questions.deep_dive:
Hybrid search combines lexical relevance and semantic relevance instead of forcing you to choose one. Keyword search is good when exact terms, filters, and field matches matter. Vector search is good when meaning matters more than literal term overlap. In practice, strong search systems often combine BM25-style text relevance, metadata filters, and vector similarity, then rerank or blend the results so you get both precision and recall.

More importantly, you can use OpenSearch’s search features to enhance the search experience. For example, you can use Learning to Rank in OpenSearch to integrate user clickthrough behavior data into your search application and improve search relevance. You can also combine OpenSearch text search and vector search capabilities to search documents with keyword and semantic similarity. You can also use other fields in the index to filter documents to improve relevance. questions.question: TurboQuant?
questions.core_answer: Google's vector compression. PolarQuant (main signal) + QJL (residual correction). 3-bit KV-cache, 6x memory reduction.
questions.deep_dive:
TurboQuant is an extreme vector-compression approach aimed at the most memory-expensive parts of AI systems, especially KV cache and vector indexes. The core idea is to preserve the comparisons that matter, such as dot products and attention logits, instead of trying to faithfully reconstruct every original float. It does that with a two-stage pipeline: PolarQuant captures most of the main signal after a random rotation, and QJL adds a tiny correction channel for the residual error. That is why it can cut memory aggressively while keeping similarity or attention quality much closer to the original system than naive low-bit storage would. questions.question: What are scalar quantization and product quantization, and when would you choose each?
questions.core_answer: Scalar quantization compresses each dimension independently and is simple to ship. Product quantization compresses subvectors with learned codebooks and usually saves more memory at scale, but it adds training and tuning complexity.
questions.deep_dive:
Scalar quantization compresses each dimension independently, so it is simple, cheap to implement, and easy to reason about. It works well when you need a straightforward memory reduction and you want to keep the indexing pipeline simple.

Product quantization splits the vector into sub-vectors and replaces each sub-vector with a codebook entry. That usually gives much better compression at larger scale, but it adds training, more tuning knobs, and an approximation layer that you need to evaluate carefully for recall.

questions.question: What is the big idea behind TurboQuant's two-stage compression?
questions.core_answer: Use most bits to capture the main signal with PolarQuant, then spend a tiny residual channel with QJL to correct hidden error. That is why it compresses hard without wrecking similarity math.
questions.deep_dive:
The big idea is to spend most of the bit budget on the main signal and a tiny additional budget on the leftover error. PolarQuant handles the main structure of the vector, while QJL uses a very cheap correction path so the final comparison stays accurate.

That is a much smarter strategy than only lowering precision everywhere equally, because the residual error is what often quietly damages dot products.

Vault Notes (from your Technical Obsidian):

Source: Technical/Artificial Intelligence/Vector Search/Opensearch/Opensearch Vector Search Notes.md
- **Euclidean distance** – The straight-line distance between points. - **L1 (Manhattan) distance** – The sum of the differences of all of the vector components. L1 distance measures how many orthogonal city blocks you need to traverse from point A to point B. - **L-infinity (chessboard) distance** – The number of moves a King would make on an n-dimensional chessboard. It’s different than Euclidean distance on the diagonals—a diagonal step on a 2-dimensional chessboard is 1.41 Euclidean units away, but 2 L-infinity units away. - **Inner product** – The product of the magnitudes of two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them. Usually used for natural language processing (NLP) vector similarity. - **Cosine similarity** – The cosine of the angle between two vectors in a vector space. - **Hamming distance** – For binary-coded vectors, the number of bits that differ between the two vectors. Advantage of OpenSearch as a vector database

The IVF algorithm separates your index vectors into a set of buckets, then, to reduce your search time, only searches through a subset of these buckets. However, if the algorithm just randomly split up your vectors into different buckets, and only searched a subset of them, it would yield a poor approximation. The IVF algorithm uses a more elegant approach. First, before indexing begins, it assigns each bucket a representative vector. When a vector is indexed, it gets added to the bucket that has the closest representative vector. This way, vectors that are closer to each other are placed roughly in the same or nearby buckets. questions.core_answer: It describes the vector in a more compression-friendly form based on magnitude and angles instead of only raw coordinates. That captures the main structure with less overhead than naive per-dimension storage.
questions.deep_dive:
PolarQuant changes how the vector is described. Instead of thinking only in raw Cartesian coordinates, it represents the data more like magnitude plus direction, which is often easier to compress with lower overhead.

In higher dimensions, the same idea is applied recursively by grouping coordinates and converting them into radii and angles. The value is that the representation becomes more structured and compressible before the residual fix-up step happens.
