The IVF algorithm separates your index vectors into a set of buckets, then, to reduce your search time, only searches through a subset of these buckets. However, if the algorithm just randomly split up your vectors into different buckets, and only searched a subset of them, it would yield a poor approximation. The IVF algorithm uses a more elegant approach. First, before indexing begins, it assigns each bucket a representative vector. When a vector is indexed, it gets added to the bucket that has the closest representative vector. This way, vectors that are closer to each other are placed roughly in the same or nearby buckets. questions.question: What is QJL doing intuitively?
questions.core_answer: QJL uses a very cheap projected sign-based representation to correct residual comparison error. It is not trying to reconstruct the whole vector perfectly; it is trying to preserve the score that matters.
questions.deep_dive:
QJL is a very cheap residual-correction trick based on projecting the data and storing an ultra-compact sign-style representation. It is not trying to perfectly rebuild the original vector. It is trying to preserve the comparison result that downstream math cares about.

That is why it fits well after PolarQuant: PolarQuant handles the bulk of the vector and QJL cleans up the residual bias that would otherwise distort attention or similarity.

questions.question: Why does TurboQuant rotate vectors before quantizing them?
questions.core_answer: Random rotation spreads information more evenly across dimensions, which makes the distribution less lopsided and easier to quantize well. It helps avoid wasting bits on a few dominant coordinates.
questions.deep_dive:
Real vectors are often lopsided: a few coordinates dominate while others are tiny, sparse, or correlated. Random rotation spreads the information more evenly across dimensions, which makes uniform quantization work much better.

In other words, the rotation is a geometry-fixing step. It makes the downstream quantizer deal with a more balanced signal instead of a few oversized coordinates that waste the bit budget.

questions.question: Why is TurboQuant useful for KV cache?
questions.core_answer: Attention repeatedly compares queries with many stored keys, so memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck. Compressing those keys aggressively lets more fit in memory and reduces the bytes moved per attention step.
questions.deep_dive:
In transformer serving, attention repeatedly compares a query against many stored keys, so the system keeps rereading large vector state from memory. That means the bottleneck is often bandwidth, not raw flops.

If you can compress the stored keys and still preserve attention logits well enough, you reduce KV-cache footprint, fit more context in memory, and spend less time moving bytes per attention step.

questions.core_answer: Similarity search cares about preserving ranking quality, not perfectly reconstructing each stored vector. If compressed vectors still produce accurate comparisons, indexes get smaller and search gets faster.
questions.deep_dive:
Vector search only cares about preserving the ranking or similarity behavior that decides which neighbors survive. If compressed vectors still preserve those comparisons, the index can become much smaller without destroying retrieval quality.

That is attractive because smaller indexes mean more vectors in RAM, lower memory cost, and faster candidate evaluation for the same hardware footprint.

questions.question: What trade-offs should you discuss when compressing KV cache?
questions.core_answer: Compression saves memory bandwidth and context cost, but too much compression can hurt attention quality, long-context behavior, or hardware efficiency. The right answer balances bit width, quality loss, and the actual serving bottleneck.
questions.deep_dive:
Compression helps when memory bandwidth or capacity is the serving bottleneck. But the trade-off is that too much compression can distort attention, especially on long-context workloads where small errors accumulate. A strong answer balances three things: how many bits you save, what quality loss appears on real prompts, and whether the hardware bottleneck is actually bandwidth, memory capacity, or compute. questions.question: How should you evaluate a RAG system in layers instead of with one vague score?
questions.core_answer: Separate retrieval quality, context construction, answer faithfulness, and user-task success. Otherwise a weak retriever and a weak generator get mixed into one number that hides the real bottleneck.
questions.deep_dive:
Evaluate RAG in layers: retrieval quality, context assembly, answer faithfulness, and end-task success. That way you can see whether the retriever missed relevant chunks, the prompt built poor context, or the model hallucinated even with decent evidence.

One single score hides the bottleneck. Layered evaluation tells you which subsystem deserves the next engineering effort.

- Every broker tiers its user partition segments and indices to a remote store - The tiering happens asynchronously and only once certain requirements are fulfilled (closed segment, LSO, indices present, etc) - The state of this tiering is kept in an internal topic named **remote_log_metadata**. - Before and after tiering, the broker writes the state of the tiering and plugin-specific metadata to the appropriate **remote_log_metadata** partitions. - The Aiven plugin stores the data in three different blobs in object storage: 1. The segment file, the largest one, is uploaded in separate chunks via multi-part PUTs. 2. A single blob consisting of all the index data, including producer snapshots and leader epoch checkpoints. 3. A manifest blob with metadata specific to the plugin, including information about the chunks. - Every broker leads some **remote_log_metadata** partitions. - Every broker actively consumes all **remote_log_metadata** partitions to build up the latest remote segment state in memory.

At any one time, there is only one so-called “active” segment. This is the open file that the latest data is appended to. After a configurable size/time threshold passes, the segment gets “closed”, and a new active one is created. When to Upload

This quick tiering behavior means that you practically won’t have more than two untiered segments at any time during stable operations. Since the copy task runs every 30 seconds and the default segment size in Kafka is 1 GiB, by the time the active segment gets closed - the previous one will likely have been uploaded.

questions.question: Which retrieval metrics matter most in practice: precision, recall, MRR, and nDCG?
questions.core_answer: Precision tells you how much returned content is relevant, recall tells you what you missed, MRR rewards getting a good hit early, and nDCG values ranking quality across the whole list. Use the metric that matches the product behavior you care about.
questions.deep_dive:
Precision tells you how much of what you returned was relevant. Recall tells you how much relevant content you missed. MRR rewards getting a strong hit very early. nDCG rewards the quality of the whole ranking while weighting top positions more heavily. The right metric depends on product behavior. If only the first result matters, MRR matters a lot. If users inspect a ranked list, nDCG is often more informative. questions.question: Why can a RAG system fail even when retrieval metrics look decent?
questions.core_answer: Retrieved passages may be individually relevant but still incomplete, conflicting, stale, or poorly assembled for the prompt. Good retrieval is necessary, not sufficient, for a grounded answer.
questions.deep_dive:
Because relevance at chunk level is not the same thing as answerability. The retrieved passages may each look relevant but still be incomplete, contradictory, stale, or poorly assembled for the prompt.

That is why strong RAG evaluation separates retriever quality from answer faithfulness. You can have acceptable retrieval numbers and still ship a bad answering system.

For a list of supported spaces, see the section for a specific engine. Note: This value can also be specified at the top level of the mapping. For more information, see Spaces. engine No faiss No The approximate k-NN library to use for indexing and search. Valid values are faiss, lucene, and nmslib (deprecated). parameters No null No The parameters used for the nearest neighbor method. For more information, see the section for a specific engine. Supported methods

The IVF algorithm separates your index vectors into a set of buckets, then, to reduce your search time, only searches through a subset of these buckets. However, if the algorithm just randomly split up your vectors into different buckets, and only searched a subset of them, it would yield a poor approximation. The IVF algorithm uses a more elegant approach. First, before indexing begins, it assigns each bucket a representative vector. When a vector is indexed, it gets added to the bucket that has the closest representative vector. This way, vectors that are closer to each other are placed roughly in the same or nearby buckets. - It must not be an active segment. (You can’t have producers actively writing to it). - Has all of the required index files created - the time index file, the offset index file, the producer snapshot index, the leader epoch index, and the transaction index. - Has not been uploaded to the external store before (obviously). - The Last Stable Offset (LSO) must have advanced beyond this file’s largest offset. - Reminder: the LSO is a composite of the High Watermark and the last (highest) committed offset for transactions - it represents the minimum of both. It basically represents the highest (latest) offset that should be visible to consumers - It’s used to ensure that all in-sync brokers have replicated the data by the time we tier it, as well as ensure that all transactions up to that point have been committed.

- Network bandwidth - the plugin sends the data to the external storage over the wire. - Disk bandwidth - the plugin needs to read the data it’s about to tier from disk. - CPU time - compressing and encrypting data can take up CPU, but even reading for disk and uploading to the external storage takes CPU, because it is not zero copy.

- The broker config can only throttle at **the segment level** - the broker only controls the decision of whether to ask the plugin to upload more segments at any given time. It cannot control whether the segment is uploaded at a high rate or not. - The plugin config has finer-grained control to limit the upload at the buffer-level of any given segment.

questions.question: Why are metadata filters still essential in a vector-search system?
questions.core_answer: Vectors capture semantic similarity, but products still need hard constraints like tenant, language, brand, freshness, or environment. The best search systems combine semantic recall with filter precision.
questions.deep_dive:
Vector similarity gives you semantic recall, not hard business constraints. Real systems still need filters for tenant, freshness, region, environment, language, or product attributes that must be obeyed exactly.

The winning design is usually semantic retrieval plus filter precision plus reranking when needed. That is what keeps vector search useful inside real products instead of toy demos.

**3. Opensearch Vector Search** We are leveraging the vector search capability of OpenSearch for storing, indexing, and searching the enriched slow log data. It uses the msmarco-distilbert-base-tas-b model from Hugging Face (Sentence-Transformers) with a vector dimension of 768. An ingest pipeline (slowlog-embedding-pipeline) automatically generates vector embeddings for both the encrypted raw log (log_vector) and the human-readable summary (summary_vector) during document ingestion. All data is indexed in a k-NN enabled index (slowlogs-search-index), and a Python script is used to efficiently bulk-upload the processed JSON documents to OpenSearch.
